original.target_description: Study 1 Pearson correlation between heart rate and anterior-posterior body sway during the angry-faces block (social-threat condition), female students; printed p.1579/PDF p.5.

n.sample_role: Female student participants contributing paired heart-rate and body-sway measures in the angry-faces block; test-specific analytic n not printed.
n.exclusions: Three excessive-movement outliers identified in Results; no correlation-specific sample count or missing-data statement printed.
n.location: Printed pp.1576–1577 (PDF pp.2–3), Method/Participants and Results; correlation on p.1579 (PDF p.5).
n.quote: Fifty female students (mean age = 20.6 years, SD = 2.3 years) were included in this study. / Three participants were identified as outliers because of their excessive movements, as reflected in Z scores greater than 4 on the body-sway measure.

es.location: Printed p.1579 (PDF p.5), left column, final paragraph before Discussion.
es.quote: Finally, there was a positive correlation between heart rate … and body sway in the angry-faces block (r = .29, p = .048),

p.location: Printed p.1579 (PDF p.5), left column, final paragraph before Discussion.
p.quote: there was a positive correlation between heart rate … and body sway in the angry-faces block (r = .29, p = .048),

replication.target_description: Replication measured heart rate but not body sway. Supplied description combines both measures and does not identify a unique test on PDF p. 4: this page includes block × STAI, angry-versus-neutral/happy contrasts, baseline and pre-block comparisons. A unique matching effect cannot be established.

reported_success.quote: While our findings are not completely in line with Roelofs et al. (2010), they support the notion that people show physiological signs of freezing in response to social threat.

notes:
Broad description and page locator do not uniquely select a statistical test; no candidate effect was arbitrarily chosen. Reported success is the authors’ overall narrative verdict; it does not establish the unidentified effect. Original full text unavailable through public routes.
Source follow-up: Published seven-page article, Facing Freeze: Social Threat Induces Bodily Freeze in Humans, Roelofs, Hagenaars, and Stins (2010), DOI 10.1177/0956797610384746; first page and PDF pages 3–5 visually inspected. The p.5 locator and angry-faces/body-sway/heart-rate description jointly identify the correlation, distinct from the neutral-faces and happy-faces correlations in the same paragraph. Requested partial eta squared is not printed for this correlation: extracted printed Pearson r without conversion. No explicit test-specific analytic n printed. Replication and reported_success intentionally unexamined under original-only assignment.
